passage:
12 Aug, night
Weird thing in class today. The monitor said we should all tell ma'am our group project was fine, so we'd get the free period. It wasn't fine. Half the volcano chart was copied off the old one in the corridor. Everyone nodded. I nodded. Then Vidya, who hardly talks, said, "But isn't it kind of copied?" Just that. Silence for maybe two seconds. Then Sameer said, "Yeah, the lava part is literally the old chart." Then Ritika agreed. Then me. I even said the colours were the same. In five minutes the whole bench had turned. We're redoing the volcano on Monday. It's like everyone was waiting for one person to go first. I wish it had been me. Tomorrow I'll tell Vidya her question helped.
Pranav

qa.q: What did Vidya ask the group?
qa.a: Vidya asked, "But isn't it kind of copied?"

qa.q: What does Pranav's line "I wish it had been me" suggest about how Pranav feels?
qa.a: Pranav seems a little ashamed of just nodding and admires the nerve it took Vidya to speak first.

qa.q: Which moment turned the group, and how could Pranav use that next time?
qa.a: Vidya's single question turned it; next time Pranav could be the first to voice a doubt, or quickly back whoever does.

qa.q: What might those two seconds of silence have been like for Vidya?
qa.a: Vidya, who hardly talks, may have felt exposed and unsure whether anyone would agree, until Sameer spoke up.

grounding: A student notices that one classmate's doubt quickly lets others disagree with the group too.

passage: The local bus from the district science fair rattled past the sugarcane fields, and the Class 10 group was loud with complaints. "The judges only liked the town schools," Bablu said. "Totally," said four voices together. Suraj, squeezed by the window, remembered their water-pump model sputtering and stopping right in front of the judges. He kept quiet. Then Wasim, holding the model on his knees, said, "But our wire came loose. They saw it stop." The bus went quiet except for the engine. Then Gudiya said, "I did tape it badly." Bablu shrugged. "And we never practised the explanation." Within five minutes they were writing a list of fixes on the back of a bus ticket. Suraj watched how fast it had turned, and how it had needed only Wasim to start.

qa.a: It sputtered and stopped, because a wire came loose.

qa.q: What turned the group from blaming to fixing, and how could Suraj use that next time?
qa.a: Wasim's honest line about the loose wire opened the door; next time Suraj could say it first, or speak up right after someone else does.

passage: The student council in Clara's school in Vienna was voting on a new rule: no phones at all during lunch, not even in bags. The class rep said, "Hands up if you agree," and hand after hand went up. Clara, fourteen, raised hers too, though she had a doubt. Then Hana, from the back, kept her hand down and said, "Wait. What about people who need to call home? My mum works nights, she texts me at lunch." The room went silent. Then Felix lowered his hand. "My little brother gets picked up by me. I need my phone." Two more hands dropped. Then Clara's. Within a minute, half the class was suggesting changes: phones allowed in bags, calls in the corridor. Clara watched it happen and thought how nobody had moved until Hana did.

qa.q: What rule was the student council voting on?
qa.a: A rule of no phones at all during lunch, not even in bags.

qa.q: What does Clara lowering her hand after Hana spoke suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests she had her own doubt all along but did not dare show it until someone else spoke first.

qa.q: What choice gave the class a better rule, and why?
qa.a: Hana's decision to keep that hand down and explain the reason gave others the support they needed to share their own concerns, so the rule could be improved.

qa.q: How might Hana have felt as the first one to disagree?
qa.a: Hana was probably nervous speaking against a room full of raised hands, and relieved when Felix and others joined in.

grounding: A student watches one classmate voice doubt about a popular rule and sees others quickly dare to disagree once they have a supporter.

passage: At the coaching centre, the whole Class 12 batch was signing a complaint against Mr Iyer, the physics teacher. "Too strict, too fast," the letter said. Thirty signatures filled the page. Jagdish, seventeen, sat by the window watching the paper go round. When it reached Hansa, she didn't sign. She said, not loudly, "Has anyone actually talked to him first? He did stay back two hours for us before the mock." Silence. Then Ravi said, "Yeah... he helped me with rotation." Another student put her pen down. "Maybe we just ask him to slow down." In five minutes the letter was folded away and three students were volunteering to speak to Mr Iyer after class. Jagdish kept thinking about it on the bus. Twenty-nine people had signed without a word. It had taken only one voice to make the others remember what they really thought.

qa.q: How many signatures were already on the complaint?
qa.a: Thirty signatures filled the page.

qa.q: What was Hansa thinking when she didn't sign?
qa.a: She was doubtful that a complaint was fair, remembering that Mr Iyer had stayed back two hours for them before the mock.

qa.q: What did the batch decide to do instead, and why was it better?
qa.a: Three students chose to speak to Mr Iyer directly and ask him to slow down, which gave him a chance to respond instead of facing a group complaint.

qa.q: How might Mr Iyer have felt if the complaint had gone ahead?
qa.a: He might have felt hurt and blindsided, especially after staying back two hours to help the students.

grounding: A student observes how one classmate's doubt about a group complaint quickly frees others to disagree with the majority.

Dear Farhan bhai,
Something interesting happened in our class debate today and I keep thinking about it.
The topic was whether we should have a longer school day. Everyone in class, and I mean everyone, voted no. Then Sir asked if anyone disagreed. Silence. I actually thought a longer day with sports might be good, but I didn't say it.
Then Anjali raised her hand and said, "I think it could help if the extra hour was for sports or clubs." The class stared. But within a minute, Deepak said, "Actually, I agree." Then two more. By the end, the vote was almost half-half.
It was like one person broke a spell. I noticed I'd only needed one other person to feel brave. Next time I want to be the Anjali.
Wasim

qa.a: She said it could help if the extra hour was for sports or clubs.

qa.a: Wasim felt hesitant and afraid to speak, even though a longer day with sports seemed good.

qa.q: What does Wasim learn from watching Anjali?
qa.a: One person voicing doubt makes it much easier for others to speak honestly, so being that first voice can help everyone.

qa.q: How might Anjali have felt when Deepak agreed with her?
qa.a: Anjali likely felt relieved and supported after the stares, no longer alone in her view.

grounding: A student notices that once one classmate voices a different view, others quickly dare to disagree, showing how one ally breaks group pressure.

passage: Amandeep, you asked how the council vote went. It was so strange. I'm Himani, and I was watching from the side as a class rep. The head boy proposed we spend the whole budget on a DJ for the fest. Everyone clapped. The teacher asked, "All agreed?" Hands went up everywhere. I saw a few people half-raise theirs, looking around. Then Tara from class eleven said, very calmly, "I think we should keep some for the library corner." For a second it was silent. Then someone else said, "Yeah, the books are falling apart." Then another. Suddenly six hands were up for the library. It was like they'd all been waiting for one person to go first. The DJ still got most of the money, but the library got some too. I've never seen a room change so fast.

passage: I sit behind Bidisha in the science club, so I saw exactly how it happened. The club leader said our project should be a volcano model. Everybody nodded. I thought a water-purifier would be more useful, but everyone looked so certain. Bidisha had her hand half up, then down, then up again. Finally she said, "Can I ask, would a water filter be more useful for our village?" There was a pause. Then Ramesh, beside me, said, "I was thinking the same thing." After that, three more people agreed. The leader said we'd vote properly. The filter won by two. I can't say what Bidisha was feeling inside, but her ears were red and she kept her eyes on her notebook. I noticed how much easier it was for the rest of us once she'd gone first.

qa.a: The club leader said the project should be a volcano model.

Wednesday: The debate came back. Jatin, who never spoke, raised his hand. "I actually like weekend homework. It's the only time I can finish things properly." The room went quiet.
Then Aadhya heard herself say, "Me too." Two more hands went up. Then five.
Friday: Aadhya wrote in her notebook: "Nobody was alone. We just didn't know till Jatin spoke."

Anand beta, you're scared to disagree in your class? Let your Nani tell you. My name is Tanuja. When I was fifteen, in the girls' hostel in Pune, a girl was caught with a transistor radio.
The senior girls called a meeting. "She should lose her Sunday outing for a month," they said. Everyone nodded. I thought it was too harsh, but I kept my mouth shut.
Then a quiet girl called Pushpa stood up. "I think a month is too much for a radio."
Silence. Then another girl said, "I agree." Then I said it. Then six more.
The punishment became one Sunday. I watched it happen and never forgot: it took one voice to crack the wall.

qa.a: The girl was caught with a transistor radio.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling before Pushpa stood up?
qa.a: Tanuja felt uneasy and afraid to speak, thinking the punishment was too harsh but keeping quiet.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the meeting, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Pushpa standing up to say a month was too much; once one girl spoke, others found it easier to agree, and the punishment was reduced.

qa.q: How might the girl with the radio have felt when the punishment became one Sunday?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and grateful that some girls spoke up for her.

grounding: Shows, as an elder's memory, a student noticing how one girl's doubt in a meeting let others dare to disagree with the majority.

The school bus was leaving in five minutes and the class had to choose: amusement park or science museum. The monitor called for hands. "Amusement park?" Almost everyone.
Uday wanted the museum, but he kept still. He could see three others shifting too.
Then Lakshmi, at the back, pushed her hair aside and said clearly, "I'd rather do the museum. There's the planetarium show."
Uday felt something loosen in his chest. "Me too," he said. Four more hands went up. Then two more.
The monitor counted again. It was nearly equal now. The teacher, checking her watch, said, "Morning museum, afternoon park."
On the bus, Uday sat beside Lakshmi. "Thanks for going first."

qa.q: What show was at the science museum?
qa.a: There was the planetarium show.

qa.q: What did Uday feel when Lakshmi spoke up?
qa.a: He felt relief and a new courage, as if something loosened in his chest.

qa.q: What does this scene show about speaking against a majority?
qa.a: One person voicing doubt can give others the courage to disagree too, so it helps to speak or to back up the first person quickly.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel when Uday thanks her on the bus?
qa.a: Lakshmi may feel pleased and less alone, knowing her words helped others.

grounding: Shows a student noticing that once one classmate voices a different choice, others quickly dare to disagree, even with little time.

passage: I'm Kalyani, and last term I was on the prefects' council. At one meeting the head prefect proposed banning Class 8 from the library's back corner because "they're noisy." Every hand went up. Mine too, halfway. Then Aparna said, very softly, "But that's the only place they can sit together. Could we just ask them to keep it down?" I remember the room going still. Then another prefect lowered his hand. Then two more. Within a minute the vote had flipped. I wasn't the one who spoke, but I watched it happen. What stayed with me was how many of us had doubts and needed just one voice before we'd admit them. Now when I disagree, I remember that I might be someone else's one voice.

qa.q: Who did the head prefect want to ban from the library's back corner?
qa.a: Class 8.

qa.q: How can you tell that Kalyani felt unsure before Aparna spoke?
qa.a: Kalyani raised a hand only halfway, which suggests hesitation and unease about the ban even while voting with everyone.

qa.q: What would you advise a prefect who disagrees but fears being alone?
qa.a: Speak up gently with a reason and an alternative, as Aparna did, because others with the same doubt often follow.

qa.q: If you were one of the Class 8 students, what would you want from the council?
qa.a: You would want to be asked to keep quiet rather than banned, and to know someone on the council stood up for your only shared space.

grounding: Illustrates a student noticing that one ally voicing doubt makes it much easier for others to disagree with the majority.

passage:
Class 10 civics note, Thursday
Today's class vote on the school's new phone rule looked unanimous at first: twenty-eight hands up for a total ban. Then Wasim slowly put his hand down and said, "I'm not sure. What about kids who travel alone by bus?" The room went quiet. Within a minute Sabina raised a doubt too, then four others, and the discussion finally became real. After class Sabina stayed back. She told me she had disagreed from the start but "couldn't be the only one". "Once Wasim said it, it was like a door opened," she said. She had counted at least six people who changed their vote only after he spoke. I thanked her for noticing. Next week I will collect private written votes first, before any hands go up.
Neelam, civics teacher

qa.q: How many hands went up for a total ban at first?
qa.a: Twenty-eight.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel before Wasim spoke, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and alone in her disagreement, saying she "couldn't be the only one", until Wasim's doubt felt like a door opening.

qa.q: What will Neelam try next week, and why?
qa.a: Private written votes before hands go up, so each student records an honest view before the pressure of the majority starts.

qa.q: What might Wasim have felt when he put his hand down?
qa.a: Wasim probably felt nervous and exposed as the first to disagree, though his doubt made it easier for others to speak.

grounding: A student notices that once one classmate voices doubt in a vote, several others quickly dare to disagree too.
